newsitem.title: LITHUANIA: FOCUS - LITHUANIAN T-BILL YIELDS SEEN FALLING.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - LITHUANIAN T-BILL YIELDS SEEN FALLING.

text.p: Yields on Lithuanian Treasury bills are seen falling as foreign investors return to the market and the country prepares a $200 million Eurobond issue.
"There is scope for further reductions if monetary policies are kept on track," said Domenico Fanizza, the International Monetary Fund's (IMF) resident representative in Lithuania.
"The rates still reflect some uncertainties about policies...what investors want is stability," he said.
"But the fall over the past year has been dramatic, and that shows that a measure of confidence has been restored," he added.
Yields soared early last year in the wake of a banking crisis to almost 40 percent, but have since fallen to a 10.50 percent to 12.0 percent range, where they have stabilized in recent weeks.

Analysts expect yields to fall some more as foreign investors begin eyeing the market again after they were scared off by an expected change to the country's currency board, which pegs the litas at a rate of four to one dollar.
The right-of-centre government headed by Gediminas Vagnorius, which was swept to power in last fall's parliamentary elections, initially vowed that it would move quickly to scrap the currency board.

Foreigners held 37.07 percent of the country's T-bills at the end of the third quarter of 1996, 33.42 percent at the end of the year, and only 26.0 percent at the end of February - a clear sign of concern about the government's monetary policies.

The government has since pledged that no hasty moves will be made to dismantle the system and the central bank has prepared a blueprint to gradually remove the currency board model in stages over a two to three year period.
"Investors have been reassured and have become more comfortable with the government's plans regarding the currency board," a London-based analyst with investment bank Merrill Lynch told Reuters.
"We still recommend Lithuanian debt paper as a good buy," he said.
"Investors are also starting to look more closely at debt in local currencies. Concerns about interest rate hikes in the U.S. have made made dollar-denominated bonds less attractive," he added.

"We see growing interest right now in our local T-bill market among foreign buyers, and that should bring yields down," said Ruta Skyriene, the deputy head of the Lithuanian foreign ministry's international department.
A group of senior fund managers recently visited Lithuania to examine the country's debt market.
She added that the country's planned $200 million Eurobond issue would also reduce domestic borrowing costs.
The issue, which will be lead managed by JP Morgan, will probably be launched early this summer after the country acquires a rating from rating agency S&P.
